fields.h1: How to Read the Bible (for Beginners)
fields.meta_title: How to Read the Bible: A Beginner’s Guide
fields.description: The Bible was given to ordinary people, not scholars. Here is how to start reading it — which book to begin with, how to read for the heart, and how to build a daily habit.
fields.body_html:
The Bible is the best-selling book in history and one of the least-read. Many people own several copies, mean to read them, and never quite know where to begin. It can look intimidating — a thick book, ancient, full of unfamiliar names and strange customs. But the Bible was given not to scholars only but to ordinary people, and God intends every believer to read it, understand it, and live by it. It is his living word, the way he speaks to us, feeds us, and guides us. Learning to read it well is the single most valuable habit a Christian can form. Here is how to begin, and how to keep going.

Know what the Bible is — and why it is worth reading

Before learning how to read the Bible, it helps to know what you are holding. The Bible is not merely a collection of ancient religious writings; it is God’s own word, “breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16). Through these pages the living God addresses you personally. That single conviction changes everything about how you approach it — not as a textbook to master but as a message from the One who made and loves you.

And it is a lamp for the journey of life: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105). In a confusing world, the Bible gives light — enough to see the next step, and the direction of the whole road. Whatever you face, the Scriptures speak into it, because their author knows the end from the beginning. To read the Bible is to let God shine his light on your way.

Start with the right book, not page one

A common mistake is to open at Genesis and try to read straight through. That works for some, but many get bogged down in the middle of the Old Testament law and give up. A better beginning for most is one of the Gospels — Mark for its briskness, or John for its depth — where you meet Jesus directly, which is what the whole Bible is finally about. Jesus himself said the Scriptures “bear witness about me” (John 5:39), and after his resurrection he showed his followers how “in all the Scriptures” the story pointed to him (Luke 24:27).

From a Gospel, move to a short letter like Philippians or 1 John, then to Acts for the story of the early church, and to the Psalms for the language of prayer. There is no single correct order, but starting where Jesus is most clearly seen gives you the key that unlocks the rest. The whole book — history, law, prophecy, poetry — finds its centre in him.

Read slowly, and aim to meet God, not just finish a chapter

The goal of Bible reading is not to cover ground but to hear from God. It is better to read a few verses thoughtfully than many carelessly. The blessed person in Psalm 1 is the one whose “delight is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he meditates day and night” (Psalm 1:2) — meditates, turning the words over slowly like a person savouring good food. Such a person becomes “like a tree planted by streams of water” (Psalm 1:3), deep-rooted and fruitful.

So read to feed, not merely to finish. Take a short passage and ask a few simple questions of it: What does this tell me about God? What does it show me about myself? Is there a promise to trust, a command to obey, an example to follow or avoid, a sin to confess? Then pause and pray it back to God. New believers are urged to crave the Scriptures the way an infant craves milk — “long for the pure spiritual milk, that by it you may grow up into salvation” (1 Peter 2:2). Read for nourishment, and you will grow.

Ask God to help you understand

The Bible is a spiritual book, and it is understood with spiritual help. You are not meant to unlock it by cleverness alone; you are meant to ask its Author to open it to you. The Psalmist prayed, “Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18) — a prayer worth breathing every time you open the book. The same Spirit who inspired the Scriptures lives in every believer to illuminate them.

So begin your reading with a short prayer: “Lord, open my eyes; speak to me; show me Jesus; change me by your word.” This lifts Bible reading out of the realm of duty and into relationship. You are not merely studying a text; you are sitting at the feet of a living Teacher who delights to make himself known. The humblest reader who prays this prayer will see more than the cleverest scholar who does not.

Read it to obey it, not just to know it

The Bible is given not merely to inform us but to transform us, and its truth is grasped most fully in the doing. James warns against a reading that never reaches the life: “be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves” (James 1:22). He compares the mere hearer to a man who glances in a mirror and immediately forgets what he looks like. The point of seeing ourselves in Scripture is to be changed by what we see.

So read with a readiness to obey. When a command convicts you, respond to it. When a promise comforts you, lean your weight on it. When a sin is exposed, confess and turn from it. This is how the word does its work — “the man who looks into the perfect law... and perseveres, being no hearer who forgets but a doer who acts, he will be blessed in his doing” (James 1:25). A little Scripture obeyed does more good than much Scripture merely admired.

What to do when a passage confuses you

Every reader of the Bible meets passages that puzzle them, and this is nothing to be ashamed of. Even the apostle Peter admitted that some of Paul’s letters contain “things in them that are hard to understand” (2 Peter 3:16). The Bible was written over many centuries in ancient cultures, so a measure of difficulty is to be expected. The key is not to let the hard parts stop you from feasting on the clear ones — and most of what you need to know is plain to any humble reader.

When you hit something confusing, try a few simple things. Read the verses around it, since context usually clears up much of the difficulty. Let the clear parts of Scripture interpret the unclear, rather than building strange ideas on a single obscure verse. Use a trustworthy study Bible or ask a mature Christian for help — in the days of Nehemiah, the Levites “gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading” (Nehemiah 8:8), and God still uses teachers to help us understand. Above all, keep a humble and prayerful heart, for the deepest things of Scripture are “spiritually discerned” (1 Corinthians 2:14) and open to those who come to obey rather than merely to critique.

Make it a daily habit — and don’t give up

Reading the Bible well is less about intensity than about consistency. A short time each day, kept up over years, will shape a soul far more than occasional marathons. Joshua was told to keep God’s word constantly before him: “This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night” (Joshua 1:8). The noble believers at Berea were commended because they were “examining the Scriptures daily” (Acts 17:11). Daily is the rhythm the Bible commends.

Pick a regular time and place, start small, and be patient with yourself. Some passages will puzzle you — that is normal; read on, and let the clear parts illuminate the harder ones. Don’t measure a day’s reading by how you felt but by whether you met with God. And let the word dwell in you richly (Colossians 3:16), carrying it into your day, returning to a verse as you work or wait. It also helps to read with others — in a church, a Bible study, or with a friend — where questions can be asked and insights shared, and where the accountability keeps us going when motivation flags. And do not be discouraged by days that feel dry; faithfulness in reading, like faithfulness in eating, is not measured by the excitement of any single meal but by the steady nourishment of a lifetime. Over time you will find the Bible is not a book you read so much as a place where you meet the living God — and once you have tasted that, you will never want to go a day without it. Open it today, ask him to speak, and begin.
